problem: Prior off-road navigation work relies on clearly delineated trails, short horizons, dense 3D maps or proxy traversability signals (IMU smoothness, velocity error), and cannot plan around large obstacles beyond sight in unknown off-trail forest terrain.
motivation: Off-road robots in forests are useful for forestry, search and rescue, and exploration, but occupancy is a poor traversability measure there (vegetation is passable, water and mud are not). The paper uses a sparse topological map with human-labeled visual traversability and learned control to avoid dense mapping and physics modeling.
key_idea: Build a GPS-anchored topological map of panoramic snapshots whose edges are labeled traversable, untraversable or unknown by a DINOv2-based network trained on human labels, navigate edges with a goal-conditioned behavior cloning policy, and explore with a frontier planner.
insight: A learned image-level 'exists a visible safe path to goal' classifier, together with replanning at every node, tolerates classification errors: false negatives are harmless because neighboring edges remain, and many false positives are recovered by the controller. The paper reports no ablations. Its one design observation is that a kinematics-based time heuristic for frontier selection reduced wasteful turning compared with Euclidean distance. Data collected semi-autonomously and relabeled through hindsight steadily improved the controller.
method: Topological map: nodes hold a global pose plus left/front/right camera images, and frontier nodes hold only a 3D point; a node is added every d=1 m and connected to neighbors within r=3 m via a k-d tree. Edges are traversable, untraversable or unknown.

Traversability network Trav_θ: frozen/pretrained DINOv2 features (384-d, 256 patches) go through three 1x1 convs down to 10-d per patch, are flattened and concatenated with the 3D goal in the camera frame, and an MLP outputs 2 logits. Edge traversability is true if either endpoint's images show a visible safe path to the other.

Human labeling: a UI shows panoramas from two nodes with the other node projected in; 3855 edges were labeled initially and 1679 more later, with labeling biased toward edges leading to frontiers to obtain more untraversable examples.

Goal-conditioned BC controller: takes a history of h=5 steps of 3 camera images, velocities and past commands plus a local-frame goal, and outputs an action sequence of length 5, executing only the first (MPC-style). It is trained with hindsight-relabeled goals sampled up to l=25 steps ahead, with linear velocity in [0,1] m/s and angular velocity in [0,1] rad/s.

Frontier exploration: an R×R occupancy grid with 2 m cells marks cells containing visited nodes as occupied, and neighbors of occupied cells become frontier nodes. The closest frontier is chosen by a turn-then-drive time estimate for a skid-steer robot, A* runs over traversable edges, and only the first waypoint is sent to the BC policy before replanning.
Iterative deployment: manual driving (8.5 km, 24 h), then semi-autonomous exploration (2 km, 10 h) with hindsight-relabeled data and new labels, followed by retraining.

setting.backbone: DINOv2 (pretrained, ViT-S 384-d) + small conv/MLP heads, separate networks for traversability and BC
setting.training_data: 8.5 km / 24 h of manual driving plus 2 km / 10 h of semi-autonomous data for BC; 3855 + 1679 human-labeled traversability edges
setting.observation: three wide-angle RGB cameras (left, front, right), velocities/IMU, RTK GPS (~1 m global localization)
setting.action_space: continuous linear (0-1 m/s) and angular (0-1 rad/s) velocity, skid-steer
setting.privileged: none (assumes global GPS localization at about 1 m precision; a human supervisor intervenes for safety)

numbers_note: No standard benchmark; results are real-world deployments on two 400 m² sites, reported as intervention counts, with confusion matrices only in a figure.
results: The system autonomously explored two unseen forest sites (Gault Nature Reserve, 400 m² each, about 700 m of travel), visiting every reachable 2×2 m cell. It needed 25 supervisor interventions: 9 from traversability false positives, 11 from BC (mostly hitting small trees), and 5 from GPS antenna clearance. No baselines were compared.
limitations: No quantitative baseline or ablation comparison; evaluation covers only two sites and counts of human interventions, and a supervisor was present throughout.

Requires GPS/RTK localization, hand-tuned d and r, and heavy human traversability labeling; viewpoint-sensitive predictions and a short 1 s controller memory cause errors, e.g. forgetting the antenna clearance.
The robot has limited mobility (cannot cross water, mud or large logs), and frontier selection is not vision-based.
builds_on: Manderson et al. hindsight-relabeled goal-conditioned BC
